# Introduction

This document contains class practices and my trials referring to the Lecturer materials

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

# 1. Introduction to R

R is a programming language used for statistical computing, data analysis, and visualization.

## 1.1 Basic calculations

```{r}
2 + 5
10 - 3
5 * 4
20 / 5
2^2
sqrt(49)
```

# 2. Data structures

## 2.1 Vectors

A vector stores elements of the same basic data type.

### Numeric vectors

```{r}
x <- c(0.6, 0.7)
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)

summary(age)
mean(age)
```

### Logical vectors

```{r}
x <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
x <- c(T, F)

x
```

### Character vectors

```{r}
x <- c("a", "b", "c")
class_gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M")

x
class_gender
```

### Integer sequences

```{r}
x <- 9:29
x
```

### Complex numbers

```{r}
x <- c(1 + 0i, 2 + 4i)
x
```

## 2.2 Matrices

A matrix stores elements of the same data type in rows and columns.

```{r}
x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
x

y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
y

x %*% y
```

## 2.3 Lists

A list can contain elements of different data types.

```{r}
x <- list(1, "a", TRUE, 1 + 4i)
x
```

## 2.4 Factors

Factors represent categorical variables.

```{r}
x <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"))
x

levels(x)
```

## 2.5 Missing values

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)

is.na(x)

x <- c(1, 2, 4, "NA", 5)
bad <- is.na(x)

print(bad)
x[!bad]
```

Notice that `"NA"` is a character string, whereas `NA` represents a missing value.

### Checking complete cases

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, 5)
y <- c("a", "b", NA, "d", NA, "f")

good <- complete.cases(x, y)
good
```

## 2.6 Type coercion

R converts elements to a common type when necessary.

```{r}
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))
```

# 3. Creating data frames

A data frame can contain different data types in separate columns.

```{r}
studentID <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
math_score <- c(12, 17, 10, 9, NA)
gender <- c("M", "F", "M", "M", "F")
it_score <- c(13, 18, 11, 10, 19)

scoredata <- data.frame(
  studentID,
  gender,
  math_score,
  it_score
)

scoredata
str(scoredata)
summary(scoredata)
```

## 3.1 Entering data manually

```{r, eval=FALSE}
data_class2 <- data.frame(
  height = numeric(0),
  weight = numeric(0),
  bmi = numeric(0)
)

data_class2 <- edit(data_class2)
```

Run this code interactively in RStudio if you want to enter data through the data editor.

# 4. Data importation

R can import data from text files, spreadsheets, statistical software, and databases.

## 4.1 Importing a text file

The original document uses a local text file containing height and weight measurements.

The following code generates example data so that this report can run without that file.

```{r}
data_class <- data.frame(
  HEIGHT = c(
    161, 155, 158, 170, 160, 156, 162, 158, 158, 167,
    160, 155, 154, 155, 157, 157, 160, 158, 160, 160,
    152, 154, 150, 161, 162, 164, 161, 155, 159, 163,
    159, 160, 158, 165, 156, 163, 155, 164, 163, 168,
    157, 164, 154
  ),
  WEIGHT = c(
    50, 49, 42, 65, 60, 52, 58, 46, 45, 51,
    60, 42, 53, 48, 48, 48, 53, 52, 51, 53,
    44, 56, 63, 52, 57, 49, 52, 54, 46, 50,
    61, 55, 45, 63, 60, 56, 52, 47, 52, 55,
    48, 58, 55
  )
)

head(data_class)
tail(data_class)
data_class[10:20, ]
```

To import the original file when you have it, use:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
data_class <- read.table(
  "class_data.txt",
  header = TRUE
)

names(data_class)
head(data_class)
tail(data_class)
```

## 4.2 Exploring built-in datasets

```{r}
data()
data("airquality")

names(airquality)
str(airquality)
head(airquality)
summary(airquality)
```

# 5. Exploratory data analysis

## 5.1 Summary statistics

```{r}
data_class

summary(data_class)
str(data_class)
```

## 5.2 Means and standard deviations

```{r}
apply(data_class, 1, mean)
apply(data_class, 2, sd)

c(
  Mean = mean(data_class$HEIGHT),
  SD = sd(data_class$HEIGHT)
)

c(
  Mean = mean(data_class$WEIGHT),
  SD = sd(data_class$WEIGHT)
)
```

# 6. Relationships between variables

## 6.1 Categorical and continuous variables

The `iris` dataset is built into R.

```{r}
data("iris")
head(iris)

mean(iris$Petal.Length)

mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "setosa"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "versicolor"])
mean(iris$Petal.Length[iris$Species == "virginica"])
```

### Grouped statistics

```{r}
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
```

### Box-and-whisker plot

```{r}
boxplot(
  Sepal.Length ~ Species,
  data = iris,
  main = "Comparison of Sepal Length by Species",
  xlab = "Species",
  ylab = "Sepal Length"
)
```

## 6.2 Relationships between categorical variables

```{r}
ucba <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)

head(ucba)

cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba)
cross

prop.table(cross, 1)
```

## 6.3 Simpson's paradox

Simpson's paradox occurs when a relationship observed in combined data disappears or reverses when the data are divided into groups.

```{r}
cross2 <- xtabs(
  Freq ~ Gender + Admit,
  data = ucba[ucba$Dept == "F", ]
)

prop.table(cross2, 1)
```

# 7. Data visualization

## 7.1 Bar charts

```{r}
dat <- read.table(
  text = "ProdA ProdB ProdC ProdD
1 110 50 60 70
2 120 50 80 65",
  header = TRUE
)

barplot(
  as.matrix(dat),
  beside = TRUE,
  col = c("red", "green"),
  main = "Product Comparison",
  xlab = "Products",
  ylab = "Values",
  legend.text = TRUE
)
```

## 7.2 Another bar chart

```{r}
dat <- read.table(
  text = "A B C D E F G
1 10 80 30 90 70 60 90
2 20 50 70 50 40 10 40
3 60 80 80 60 60 30 160
4 20 40 70 80 20 10 70",
  header = TRUE
)

barplot(
  as.matrix(dat),
  main = "Comparison of Categories",
  xlab = "Categories",
  ylab = "Values",
  beside = TRUE
)
```

## 7.3 Scatter plots

```{r}
plot(
  WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT,
  data = data_class,
  main = "Weight versus Height",
  xlab = "Height",
  ylab = "Weight"
)

plot(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)

plot(
  data_class[, 1],
  data_class[, 2],
  main = "Height and Weight"
)

cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)
```

## 7.4 Histograms

```{r}
hist(
  data_class$HEIGHT,
  main = "Distribution of Height",
  xlab = "Height"
)

hist(
  data_class$WEIGHT,
  main = "Distribution of Weight",
  xlab = "Weight",
  col = "blue"
)
```

# 8. Linear models

## 8.1 Fitting a linear regression model

```{r}
plot(
  WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT,
  data = data_class,
  main = "Linear Regression: Weight and Height",
  xlab = "Height",
  ylab = "Weight"
)

model1 <- lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)

abline(model1, lwd = 2)

summary(model1)
```

## 8.2 Predicting height from weight

```{r}
data_lm <- lm(HEIGHT ~ WEIGHT, data = data_class)

summary(data_lm)
```

## 8.3 Regression diagnostic plots

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(data_lm)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 8.4 Linear regression and a smooth curve

```{r}
plot(
  WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT,
  data = data_class,
  main = "Linear and Smoothed Relationships",
  xlab = "Height",
  ylab = "Weight"
)

abline(
  lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class),
  col = "red"
)

lines(
  lowess(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT),
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2
)

cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)

lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
```

# 9. Data management

## 9.1 Creating a new variable: BMI

Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared.

\[
BMI = \frac{Weight\ (kg)}{Height\ (m)^2}
\]

```{r}
BMI <- data_class$WEIGHT /
  (data_class$HEIGHT / 100)^2

BMI

BMI <- round(
  data_class$WEIGHT /
    (data_class$HEIGHT / 100)^2,
  digits = 2
)

BMI
```

### Adding BMI to the data frame

```{r}
head(cbind(data_class, BMI), n = 5)

new_data_class <- cbind(data_class, BMI)

tail(new_data_class, n = 10)
```

## 9.2 Summary of BMI

```{r}
summary(BMI)

stem(BMI, scale = 2)
```

# 10. Working with dates

## 10.1 Today's date

```{r}
today <- Sys.Date()

format(today, format = "%B %d %Y")
format(today, format = "%A")
```

## 10.2 Calculating age in days

```{r}
today <- Sys.Date()
dob <- as.Date("1982-02-10")

difftime(today, dob, units = "days")
```

## 10.3 Difference between two dates

```{r}
startdate <- as.Date("2004-02-13")
enddate <- as.Date("2011-01-22")

days <- enddate - startdate
days
```

# 11. Subsetting and data cleaning

## 11.1 Creating a leadership dataset

```{r}
manager <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
country <- c("US", "US", "UK", "UK", "UK")
gender <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F")
age <- c(32, 45, 25, 39, 99)

q1 <- c(5, 3, 3, 3, 2)
q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2)
q3 <- c(5, 2, 5, 4, 1)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 5, NA, 2)
q5 <- c(5, 5, 2, NA, 1)

leadership <- data.frame(
  manager,
  country,
  gender,
  age,
  q1, q2, q3, q4, q5
)

str(leadership)
names(leadership)
```

## 11.2 Handling missing values

In this example, the value 99 is treated as a missing age.

```{r}
leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA
```

### Creating age categories

```{r}
leadership$agecat <- NA_character_

leadership$agecat[
  leadership$age > 75
] <- "Elder"

leadership$agecat[
  leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75
] <- "Middle Aged"

leadership$agecat[
  leadership$age < 35
] <- "Young"

leadership
```

### Identifying missing values

```{r}
is.na(leadership[, 5:9])
```

### Removing rows with missing values

```{r}
newdata <- na.omit(leadership)
newdata
```

`na.omit()` removes rows containing missing values in any column.

# 12. Sorting data

```{r}
order(leadership$age)

newdata2 <- leadership[
  order(leadership$age),
]

newdata2
```

# 13. Merging data frames

The `merge()` function joins data frames horizontally using common key columns.

For example:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
merge(dataframeA, dataframeB, by = "ID")

merge(
  dataframeA,
  dataframeB,
  by = c("ID", "country")
)
```

The `rbind()` function combines data frames vertically when their columns are compatible.

```{r}
data1 <- data.frame(
  ID = c(1, 2),
  score = c(12, 15)
)

data2 <- data.frame(
  ID = c(3, 4),
  score = c(18, 20)
)

rbind(data1, data2)
```

# 14. Selecting variables and observations

## 14.1 Selecting columns

```{r}
newdata3 <- leadership[, 5:9]
newdata3

myvars <- c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")

newdata3 <- leadership[myvars]
newdata3
```

## 14.2 Removing columns

```{r}
newdata4 <- leadership[, c(-1, -2)]
newdata4

newdata5 <- leadership[, c(-1, -7)]
newdata5
```

## 14.3 Accessing a column

```{r}
leadership[[4]]

leadership$age
```

Both expressions access the age column.

## 14.4 Selecting rows

```{r}
newdata6 <- leadership[c(2, 4, 5), ]

newdata6
```

## 14.5 Selecting rows using conditions

```{r}
newdata7 <- subset(
  leadership,
  age >= 35 | age < 24,
  select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5)
)

newdata7
```

### Selecting male managers older than 30

```{r}
newdata8 <- subset(
  leadership,
  gender == "M" & age > 30
)

newdata8
```
